A 40-year-old woman with a 5-year history of chronic hepatitis B infection is admitted to the hospital
due to 4 days of jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and nonbloody vomiting. She denies taking any medications
but reports a recent relapse into alcohol use, consuming "three or four shots a day," as well as ongoing
intravenous heroin use. She has not taken acetaminophen. Her vital signs are stable, and physical
examination reveals icterus. Abdominal examination shows a smooth liver edge at the right costal
margin without evidence of splenomegaly or ascites. No rashes or spider angiomas are observed.
Laboratory studies reveal the following results: | | Patient value | Reference range | | --- | --- | --- | |
Alanine aminotransferase (U/L) | 1340 | 0–35 | | Aspartate aminotransferase (U/L) | 1078 | 0–35 | |
Alkaline phosphatase (U/L) | 239 | 30–120 | | Total bilirubin (mg/dL) | 9.0 | 0.3–1.0 | | Albumin (g/dL) |
3.9 | 3.5–5.5 | Hepatitis serology results are as follows: - Hepatitis A virus: IgM-negative; IgG-positive -
Hepatitis B virus: surface antigen-positive; core IgG antibody-positive; core IgM antibody-negative; e

antigen-negative; and HBV DNA viral load 1400 IU/mL - Hepatitis C virus: antibody-negative;
RNA-negative A serum acetaminophen level is undetectable. What is the most likely diagnosis in this
patient? Answer Choices: (A) Acute hepatitis A virus infection (B) Chronic hepatitis B virus
exacerbation (C) Acute hepatitis C virus infection (D) Alcoholic hepatitis (E) Hepatitis B virus
reactivation (F) Hepatitis D virus infection (G) Drug-induced liver injury (H) Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
(I) Autoimmune hepatitis (J) Wilson disease
 A. Wilson disease
B. Drug-induced liver injury
C. Chronic hepatitis B virus exacerbation
D. Alcoholic hepatitis
E. Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
F. Hepatitis D virus infection
G. Acute hepatitis A virus infection
H. Autoimmune hepatitis
I. Acute hepatitis C virus infection
J. Hepatitis B virus reactivation
